scenarios.title: Route and query params
scenarios.description: GET /users/42?fields=a,b echoes the id as a number and the fields as a list.

scenarios.title: Validated JSON body
scenarios.description: POST /echo with a ~1 KB JSON body; name (string) and age (number) are validated, the reply echoes them.

scenarios.title: Server-rendered page
scenarios.description: GET /page renders a layout (head, nav, footer) and a list of 100 rows of escaped text.

scenarios.title: Auth middleware
scenarios.description: GET /secure behind an auth check on the Authorization header (a guard in yerd and Nest, a hook or middleware elsewhere).

notes: Single process per server, no clustering. Client and server run on the same machine, so absolute numbers are machine-bound; compare ratios.
Each scenario: 3s warmup, then 3 runs of 10s with 100 connections in total, pipelining 1, keep-alive on. The run with the median req/s is reported. MB/s is decimal (10^6 bytes).

The client is 4 autocannon instances in worker threads sharing the 100 connections, started together and summed: a single autocannon thread tops out around 125k req/s on this machine, which capped the fastest servers. p50/p99 are computed from every 2xx response's own time (autocannon's histogram rounds to whole milliseconds).
Every server runs with NODE_ENV=production and request logging off (yerd: logging({ filter: "warn" }); Fastify: logger false; Nest: logger false; the others log nothing by default).

Validation for POST /echo: yerd a DTO class with is.string()/is.number() via @body; Fastify a JSON schema (Ajv); Nest class-validator DTO through the global ValidationPipe; Express, Koa, Hono and the node:http baseline the same small hand-written check. Every server rejects an invalid body with 400 before measuring.
Body parsing: Express express.json(), Koa @koa/bodyparser, Hono c.req.json(), Fastify and Nest Fastify's built-in parser, yerd its built-in body reader.

SSR engine for /page: yerd TSX (its own JSX runtime, layout + route); Hono hono/jsx; Express, Fastify, Koa and Nest React 19 renderToString from react-dom/server. node:http concatenates template strings. Markup sizes are checked to be within 3% of each other.
yerd streams pages (chunked transfer encoding); the React-based servers and Hono send one buffered string with a content-length.

Per request yerd also builds a request context, creates the route class instance through its DI container in a request scope (C#-style scoped lifetime), resolves decorated accessors, and adds an x-content-type-options: nosniff header. Express adds an ETag on res.json/res.send by default; kept, since it is the default.

The auth check compares the Authorization header with a fixed token: a createGuard guard in yerd, a CanActivate guard in Nest, a route onRequest hook in Fastify, route middleware in Express, Koa and Hono.
NestJS 12.1.3 uses @nestjs/platform-fastify (which pins its own Fastify, 5.12.5). Hono runs on @hono/node-server 2.1.5. Koa uses @koa/router 15.7.0 and @koa/bodyparser 6.1.0. React 19.3.1.
node:http (baseline) is not a framework: a hand-rolled router on plain node:http, shown as a ceiling. 'vs best' percentages compare frameworks only.
CPU pinning (taskset): each server on CPUs 8,9, the client on CPUs 10-15, so results don't swing with where the scheduler puts them.

Run-to-run noise: between two full runs on this machine most cells moved by about 10% or less (yerd params by 14%); the first of those runs also had one outlier, yerd ssr 26% low while other work was running on the host, so it was run again. Treat gaps under ~10% as ties. The benchmark itself keeps 5-6 threads busy (server plus client), which is most of the load average during a run.
1-minute/5-minute/15-minute load average: 2.27 3.01 3.56 at start, 5.05 5.65 5.14 at end.
